title: Social Listening Pricing Benchmarks 2026: What Brands Actually Pay by Tier
summary: No survey tracks social listening spend. We pulled Vendr contract data and vendor rate cards across 17 tools to show what brands actually pay by tier.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** No credible industry survey tracks what brands actually spend on social listening tools — the closest thing, a Forrester report on the total cost of listening, is paywalled and dated 2016. So this benchmark is built from what's verifiable instead: vendor rate cards where they're public, and Vendr procurement data, G2 estimated-price tools, and named customer reviews where they aren't. The pattern that falls out: Entry/SMB tools run $29-$599/month and are mostly self-serve; mid-market tools publish per-seat prices but their real contract values (once social listening is added) land closer to $18,000-$50,000/year; and enterprise tools are uniformly quote-only, with confirmed median contract values ranging from about $12,600/year (Cision) to $165,000/year (Khoros). 2026 also brought real structural change: Mention was absorbed into Agorapulse through court-ordered receivership, Khoros was acquired by IgniteTech and its pricing page now redirects to a rebranded domain, and NetBase Quid relaunched as "Quid" with a pricing model built around outcomes rather than seats.


Ask five vendors for a quote and you'll get five different answers, none of which appear on their websites. That's not an accident — enterprise social listening pricing is opaque by design, and most "compare pricing" roundups just reprint whatever number a vendor's marketing page happens to show, which is usually nothing.


We went a different way: pull vendor pricing pages directly, then cross-check against Vendr's procurement database, G2's crowdsourced price-estimate tool, and named customer reviews on TrustRadius and Capterra — the actual paper trail of what real contracts cost, not just what a sales page claims. The result splits cleanly into three tiers, and a few 2026-specific stories worth knowing before you sign anything. For the vertical-specific version of this question, see our breakdowns for[consumer goods](https://syncly.app/blog/best-social-listening-tools-consumer-goods-brands-2026) ,[beauty](https://syncly.app/blog/best-social-listening-tools-beauty-brands-2026) ,[fashion](https://syncly.app/blog/best-social-listening-tools-fashion-brands-2026) , and[food & beverage](https://syncly.app/blog/best-social-listening-tools-food-beverage-brands-2026) brands.


## Is there real data on what brands spend on social listening tools?


Not really — and that gap is itself the finding. Forrester's *"The Total Cost Of Social Listening"* report is the only research we found that directly targets this question, but it's based on a 2015 survey, was published in 2016, and sits behind a $1,495 paywall (Source:[Forrester, 2016](https://www.forrester.com/report/The-Total-Cost-Of-Social-Listening/RES55266) ). Every current marketing-industry survey we checked — G2's 2026 Buyer Behavior Report, HubSpot's 2026 State of Marketing, Social Media Examiner's 2026 Industry Report — either has no listening-specific breakout or doesn't mention the category at all.


**List price vs. actual contract value (ACV)** : the list price is the number on a vendor's marketing page (if one exists); the actual contract value is what a real buyer signs for, after negotiation, add-ons, and multi-year discounts. For self-serve tools these are usually the same. For anything quote-only, they can differ by 2-5x.


Category-size estimates don't converge either, because "social listening," "media monitoring," and "social media management" get defined differently by different research firms. Grand View Research put the social listening market at $9.15 billion in 2024, growing at a 14.3% CAGR through 2030 (Source:[Grand View Research, 2025](https://www.giiresearch.com/report/grvi1728472-social-media-listening-market-size-share-trends.html) ). The Business Research Company's newer estimate puts 2026 alone at $12.15 billion, growing 17.1% annually (Source:[The Business Research Company, 2026](https://www.thebusinessresearchcompany.com/report/social-media-listening-global-market-report) ). Fortune Business Insights, using the broader "media monitoring tools" category, comes in lower at $7.34 billion for 2026 (Source:[Fortune Business Insights, 2026](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/media-monitoring-tools-market-104157) ). The spread — roughly $6.3 billion to $12.15 billion depending on category definition — is real and worth citing honestly rather than averaging into a false-precision number.

Mention is the story in this tier. It used to be the cheapest self-serve option here — Solo, Pro, and Pro Plus tiers ran $49-$179/month. In April 2025, Agorapulse acquired Mention through what its own announcement describes as a distressed, court-ordered receivership process, not a standard acquisition (Source:[Agorapulse, 2025](https://www.agorapulse.com/blog/agorapulse-news/mention-by-agorapulse-why-were-investing-in-social-listening/) ). By July 2025, the old self-serve tiers were gone, replaced by a single $599/month, annual-only "Company Plan" — a five-fold jump from its old entry price into something that behaves more like a mid-market contract. Then on January 30, 2026, Mention retired its publishing and engagement features entirely, pointing customers who need that functionality to a separate Agorapulse subscription (Source:[checkthat.ai, 2026](https://checkthat.ai/brands/mention/pricing) ). A tool that was once a budget all-in-one is now a single-purpose, higher-priced listening product.


YouScan has a smaller but telling inconsistency: its own January 2026-updated blog post about the "Starter 3" plan still quotes $299/month, while its live pricing page and Capterra both show $499/month (Source:[YouScan blog](https://youscan.io/blog/starter-3-affordable-pricing-plan/) ;[Capterra](https://www.capterra.com/p/173036/YouScan/pricing/) ). It's a small thing, but it's a useful reminder to check a vendor's actual checkout flow, not just its content marketing, before budgeting.


## What do brands actually pay for mid-market and enterprise social listening tools?


This is where "published price" and "actual contract value" diverge hardest — and where tier labels stop meaning much, because a nominally "mid-market" tool's real contract can cost more than a nominally "enterprise" one.


**Mid-market tools publish per-seat prices, but listening is usually a paid add-on that isn't priced anywhere.** Sprout Social lists Standard/Professional/Advanced at $199-$399 per seat per month, but Premium Analytics and Listening are separate add-ons with no public price — Vendr's own procurement notes state that "Social Listening in particular can double or triple total contract value" (Source:[Vendr, Sprout Social](https://www.vendr.com/marketplace/sprout-social) ). Agorapulse's Advanced Listening add-on is the same story: named on the pricing page, priced nowhere. Brandwatch and Talkwalker, by contrast, are fully quote-only from the first dollar — but Vendr's confirmed procurement data puts Brandwatch's median actual contract at **$50,000/year** , with a range of $19,542-$81,200 (Source:[Vendr, Brandwatch](https://www.vendr.com/marketplace/brandwatch) ), which is squarely enterprise money despite Brandwatch's frequent "mid-market" framing.

Two things worth flagging honestly. First, Sprinklr's actual-pay figures conflict more than any other vendor in this research: Vendr's average contract value is $127,490, while SpendHound's enterprise-customer average is $606,905 — nearly a 5x gap between two procurement-data firms (Source:[Vendr](https://www.vendr.com/marketplace/sprinklr) ; SpendHound). Neither is obviously wrong; they likely reflect different customer segments in each firm's dataset. Second, Meltwater has the richest evidence of any vendor here because real, named reviewers disclosed real numbers: one Allegion PLC manager cited $51,000/year, a small PR firm cited $3,000/year, and one Trustpilot reviewer described a mid-contract currency switch from CAD to USD that produced a "25+ percent jump in price" at renewal (Source:[Trustpilot](https://www.trustpilot.com/review/meltwater.com) ; TrustRadius).


## What pricing changes happened in the social listening market in 2026?


Three stories this year are bigger than a line-item price change — they're structural.


1.


**NetBase Quid dropped seat- and module-based pricing entirely.** Rebranded simply as "Quid," the company's February 2026 platform launch came with a direct quote from its own press release: *"We don't charge for seats, and we don't charge for modules; customers pay us for results"* (Source:[Quid, 2026](https://www.quid.com/quid-launches-q-platform-q-access-and-q-agents-to-power-enterprise-grade-consumer-and-market-insights) ). That's a genuine departure from how every other vendor in this list prices — worth watching if it becomes a trend rather than an outlier.


2.


**Khoros was acquired by IgniteTech in May 2025** , and by the time we checked in September 2026, khoros.com's pricing page was actively redirecting to a rebranded khoros.ai domain. Vendr's procurement data shows Khoros's median actual contract climbing to roughly $165,000/year — among the highest confirmed figures in this research — alongside reported layoffs at the company.


3.


**Digimind no longer exists as a standalone brand.** It's now "Onclusive Social," under parent company Onclusive, and the legacy digimind.com marketing domain forwards entirely to Onclusive's news site. On March 12, 2026, Onclusive launched a "Unified Platform" merging monitoring, measurement, and workflow into one login — a real, dated restructuring, though the announcement disclosed no pricing changes (Source:[Onclusive, 2026](https://news-en.onclusive.com/news/onclusive-launches-unified-platform-bringing-monitoring-measurement-and-workflow-capabilities-together-in-one-connected-experience) ).


If you're currently on Khoros, Digimind, or Mention specifically, a vendor-stability check belongs in your 2026 renewal conversation regardless of price. See our breakdowns of[Khoros alternatives](https://syncly.app/blog/khoros-alternatives-for-enterprise-teams) and[Digimind alternatives](https://syncly.app/blog/digimind-alternatives-for-budget-conscious-enterprise-teams) for what teams are actually switching to.


## How should a brand budget for a social listening tool in 2026?


Start from your actual buying motion, not the tier label a vendor gives itself. If a tool lets you sign up with a credit card, budget $29-$600/month depending on volume and platform coverage (Awario, Brand24, Determ). If you need a full social suite with listening bolted on as an add-on, budget the base per-seat price plus 50-100% for the add-on itself — Sprout Social and Agorapulse both fall here, and neither discloses the add-on price up front, so ask for it in writing before you sign. If you're evaluating a fully quote-only enterprise platform, use the Vendr-confirmed figures above as your opening anchor in negotiation, not the number a salesperson leads with — Vendr's own data shows buyers routinely negotiate 14-30% off list depending on the vendor.


One negotiation lever worth knowing: several vendors in this research (Meltwater, Cision, Sprinklr) build automatic annual price escalators into renewal terms, sometimes 5-15% per year, sometimes triggered by a currency-billing switch rather than a stated increase. Read the renewal clause before you sign the first contract, not when the second invoice arrives.


## Key Takeaways


-


No credible industry survey tracks actual social listening spend — the only report that tried is a paywalled 2016 Forrester study, so every figure in this piece comes from vendor pricing pages, Vendr procurement data, and named customer reviews instead.


-


Entry/SMB tools ($29-$599/month) are genuinely self-serve and transparent; Mention is the exception, having gone from a $49/month self-serve tier to a $599/month annual-only demo-gated plan after its 2025 acquisition.


-


Mid-market vendors publish per-seat prices, but social listening itself is usually an unpriced add-on that can double or triple the real contract value — ask for that number before you sign.


-


Enterprise tools are uniformly quote-only, with confirmed actual contract values ranging from roughly $12,600/year (Cision) to $165,000/year (Khoros) — a 13x spread that a list-price comparison alone would never surface.


-


Three 2026 structural changes are worth tracking regardless of your current vendor: NetBase Quid's shift to outcomes-based pricing, Khoros's post-acquisition instability, and Digimind's full absorption into Onclusive Social.


Pricing transparency in this category isn't going to improve on its own — enterprise vendors have no incentive to publish numbers that would let a prospect walk into a sales call already knowing the real range. Until that changes, the closest thing to ground truth is what's outlined above: real procurement data, named customer disclosures, and an honest accounting of where the evidence runs thin.
